course.title: Writing Longer Pieces
course.description: How to plan, build, revise and finish an essay or report: the question, the thesis, structure, paragraphs, evidence, objections, revision, and the numbers and layout of a report.
course.audience: A capable adult who writes sentences and short paragraphs well and wants to sustain an argument over several pages. They have read the English course on reading, writing and rhetoric. Taking Reading and Research first is useful but not required.

paragraphs: A sentence can be good and a paragraph can be good, and a ten-page essay can still fall apart, because most of the problems of a long piece belong to the whole. The reader can't tell what question it answers, its thesis says nothing a sensible person would dispute, or a section that reads well does nothing to prove the claim. None of these is fixed by choosing better words, which is why a writer can polish every sentence and still hand in pages that read smoothly and argue nothing.

What holds a long piece together is a handful of decisions made around the drafting, about who the piece is for, what exactly it claims and what a fair critic would say back. The useful thing about these decisions is that you can check them, often with nothing more than a list or some arithmetic. Write one line for each paragraph of a draft and you can see where the argument repeats itself, and set a word count against the claims and you can see whether the thesis is too big for the space.

Once you can make those checks, you can say why a draft is weak instead of only feeling that it is, and you can fix it in the place where the fault actually is. That holds for an essay written to persuade a tutor and for a report written for a manager who has ten minutes before a meeting, although the two put their answer in very different places.
outcomes: You'll be able to state a piece's reader, question and thesis.
You'll be able to order sections for an essay and for a decision report.
You'll be able to write paragraphs that each make one claim and explain their evidence.
You'll be able to state the strongest objection and qualify your claim.
You'll be able to revise from argument down to sentence and plan the work backwards from a deadline.
You'll be able to present numbers in a report so that text, table and figure agree.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on English: Reading, Writing and Rhetoric.

modules.title: Plan the piece
modules.description: Know the reader and the question, turn a topic into a claim worth arguing, and choose a structure before drafting.

modules.title: Build it
modules.description: Paragraphs that each do one job, evidence that is explained, objections that are answered, and ways in and out that connect.

modules.title: Revise it
modules.description: Revise from the whole to the sentence, cut what does not work, and run a process that finishes on time.

modules.title: Reports

concepts.title: Purpose
concepts.summary: What the piece is meant to make its reader know, believe or do.

concepts.title: Form
concepts.summary: The kind of piece, such as an argumentative essay or a decision report, which sets the reader's expectations.

concepts.title: Word budget
concepts.summary: A plan for how many words each part of the piece gets.

concepts.title: Topic
concepts.summary: A subject area, such as street trees.

concepts.title: Research or guiding question
concepts.summary: A question about the topic that the piece will answer.

concepts.title: Thesis
concepts.summary: A one-or-two sentence answer to the question that can be argued with evidence.

concepts.title: Outline
concepts.summary: A plan of the piece's sections and the point each makes.

concepts.title: Answer first
concepts.summary: Opening with the conclusion and then supporting it, so a reader who stops early still has the answer.

concepts.title: Order of claims
concepts.summary: Arranging the points by logic, time, importance or a chain of cause.

concepts.title: Topic sentence
concepts.summary: A sentence, usually first, that states the paragraph's one claim.

concepts.title: Unity
concepts.summary: Every sentence in the paragraph supports its one claim.

concepts.title: Coherence
concepts.summary: The sentences follow each other so that a reader can see how they connect.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.summary: Data, a quotation, an example or an authority that supports a claim.

concepts.title: Analysis
concepts.summary: The writer's explanation of what the evidence shows and why it supports the claim.

concepts.title: Signal phrase
concepts.summary: A phrase that introduces a source, such as 'According to the survey'.

concepts.title: Counterargument
concepts.summary: A reason a reasonable reader might give against your thesis.

concepts.title: Concession
concepts.summary: Granting what is right in the objection.

concepts.title: Qualifier
concepts.summary: A word or phrase that limits a claim, such as 'in hot climates' or 'usually'.

concepts.title: Transition
concepts.summary: A word or phrase that tells the reader how a sentence relates to the one before.

concepts.title: Opening
concepts.summary: The move that brings the reader from their world to your question and thesis.

concepts.title: Ending
concepts.summary: The move that says what follows from the argument and not merely what was said.

concepts.title: Reverse outline
concepts.summary: A list of what each paragraph of a draft actually says, made after the draft.

concepts.title: Global and local revision
concepts.summary: Global revision changes the argument and structure; local revision changes sentences and words.

concepts.title: Revision order
concepts.summary: Revising argument first, then structure, paragraphs, sentences and proofreading.

concepts.title: Nominalisation
concepts.summary: Turning an action into a noun, as in 'make a decision' for 'decide'.

concepts.title: Actors and actions
concepts.summary: A clear sentence puts the actor in the subject and the action in the verb.

concepts.title: Economy
concepts.summary: Using only the words the meaning needs.

concepts.title: Backward plan
concepts.summary: A schedule built from the deadline back to the start.

concepts.title: Feedback
concepts.summary: A reader's response to the piece; the most useful kind answers a question you asked.

concepts.title: Proofreading
concepts.summary: A last pass for errors, done after all other revision and on the page or aloud.

concepts.title: Executive summary
concepts.summary: A short opening section giving the question, finding and recommendation so a reader can act without reading further.

concepts.title: IMRaD
concepts.summary: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion: the usual order of a research report.

concepts.title: Signpost heading
concepts.summary: A heading that says what the section tells the reader, not only its topic.

concepts.title: Percent change
concepts.summary: (New - old) / old, expressed as a percentage.

concepts.title: Percentage points
concepts.summary: The difference between two percentages, which is not the same as percent change.

concepts.title: Caption
concepts.summary: A line that tells the reader what the figure shows and what to notice.

lessons.title: Reader, purpose and form

steps.headline: A piece of writing is built around the reader it is for and the question that reader wants answered.

lead.text: Look back at the two grids in the opening figure. Each begins with the same two rows, the **reader** and the question, and everything below them follows from those two. The tutor wants to see you take a position on whether price is the right way to choose, and to see how well you defend it. The manager wants to know what to do, and wants it before the meeting.

What the reader should know, believe or do when they finish is the piece's **purpose**. Notice that the purpose is stated from the reader's side: it isn't "to show everything I found out about suppliers". That is the commonest way a long piece goes wrong, because material that is interesting to the writer is not necessarily material that answers the question.

afterFigure.text: So before drafting, write the purpose as a sentence you could say to the reader: "By the end you'll know whether to switch." If you can't finish that sentence, you don't yet know what to include, and a longer draft won't fix it. If you *can* finish it, you now have a test for every paragraph that follows: does it help the reader reach that end?

reveal.text: The brief asks for a recommendation that someone will act on, which is what separates a report from an essay.

steps.headline: An essay builds a line of argument for a reader who asked what you think and why, and a report gives a reader the finding they need in order to decide.

lead.text: Both forms answer a question, so it's easy to treat them as one form in different clothes. They aren't, and the difference is in where the answer sits. An **essay** is a line of argument: the reader asked "what do you think, and why?", so you state your answer and then earn it, one reason at a time, and the reader is persuaded as they move through the pages in order.

A **report** serves a reader who has to *do* something. They may read only the first page, or only the first paragraph, and they still need to be able to act. So a report puts the answer first and the support behind it, in the order of how much the reader needs it.

afterFigure.text: Look at the two stacks in the figure. Both have three blocks, but you could cut the essay's last block and lose its point, whereas the report's last block can be left unread without changing what the reader decides. Writing a report as if it were an essay is a real and common fault, and it costs the busy reader the one thing they came for.

diagram.alt: Two stacks of three blocks showing reading order. The essay stack runs introduction, body, conclusion, with the answer built up along the way. The report stack runs answer, findings, detail, so the reader can stop after the first block.
diagram.caption: Both forms have three blocks, but the answer sits in a different place. Use the buttons to switch forms.

reveal.text: Covering everything describes the material, whereas the purpose describes the effect on the reader, and the two can differ a lot.

steps.headline: A word budget divides the total length among the parts of the piece before you write them.

lead.text: Once you know the form, you can decide how much room each part gets. A **word budget** is a plan for how many words each part receives, and you set it from the total you were given. Take a 3,000-word essay. A common split gives the introduction 10% and the conclusion 10%, which leaves the body 80%.

Percentages are useful here because the same split works for any length. Ten percent of 3,000 is 300 words, so the introduction and the conclusion take 300 each, and the body keeps 2,400. If the body has four sections of equal weight, each gets 600 words.

afterFigure.text: The reason to do this *before* writing is that sections expand to fill whatever room is left, and a writer who starts without a plan usually reaches the end of the allowance with the argument half made. The budget is a plan, not a rule: you can move 100 words from one section to another, but you do it on purpose and you keep the total.

workedSteps.text: Add the two fixed shares and take them from the whole to find the body's share.
Turn the body's share into words.
Each of the four sections gets a quarter of the body.
Check that the parts add back to the total.

steps.headline: Now set the budget for a 2,000-word essay with a 15% introduction, a 10% conclusion and three equal body sections.

workedSteps.text: The fixed shares are 15% and 10%, so the body gets the rest.
In words, the body is 75% of 2,000.
Three equal sections share it. Work out the length of each.

steps.headline: A budget also tests the question, because a question that needs more words than the budget allows is too big for the piece.

lead.text: The budget does a second job that people often miss. Suppose your 1,000-word essay has 800 words for its body, and your plan lists eight points you want to make. Eight points in 800 words is 100 words each, about one short paragraph, and a point that has to be explained and supported usually needs more than that.

When the sums don't work, you have two honest choices. You can cut the plan down to the points that answer the question, or you can narrow the question itself so that fewer points are needed. What you can't do is hope the points will shrink to fit, because they won't, and the piece ends up listing claims without ever supporting them.

afterFigure.text: This is also why the grid in the first figure has a row for length. Length belongs with the reader and the question, because all three decide what the piece can honestly contain.

reveal.text: The summary comes first because the reader may read nothing else, so it is worth planning its length as carefully as the body's.
Eight points in 800 words leaves about 100 words each, so either the points or the question has to get smaller.

blocks.text: Here are two briefs on the same subject, a company's choice of packaging supplier. A tutor on a business course asks "Is price the right way to choose a supplier?" and expects a position defended over several pages, while a manager at the company asks "Should we switch?" and expects the answer in the first line, because she has a decision to make this week.

You'd draw on the same facts for both, yet the two pieces would differ in their first sentence, in the order of their parts and in their length. So what decides the shape of a long piece, if it isn't the topic? Once you can name who will read it, the question they want answered and the room you have, you can tell before you write a word which form the piece should take and how many words each part of it deserves.

recap.keyIdea: A long piece starts from its reader and the question they want answered, takes the form that suits them, and divides its length among its parts before any drafting.

blocks.text: The reader's question and the piece's purpose come first, and they decide the form: an essay argues a position in order, while a report puts the finding up front for someone who has to act. Once the form is chosen, a word budget turns the total length into a length for each part, and checking that budget against the question tells you whether the question is small enough to answer.

lessons.title: From topic to thesis

steps.headline: A topic is only an area to write about, and a question is what turns it into something a piece can answer.

lead.text: Take the topic from the opening figure, street trees. You could write for hours about them and never say anything, because a topic gives you somewhere to look but nothing to find. A **topic** is a subject area, and the trouble with starting from it is that every fact about trees seems equally relevant, so the draft becomes a pile of them.

A **guiding question** fixes that. "Do street trees reduce heat illness?" picks out one corner of the topic and makes everything else either relevant to it or not. Notice how much easier the next decision becomes: you now know which sources to read, which facts to keep and which interesting ones to leave out.

afterFigure.text: You can usually find a question by asking what a reader would want to know, or what puzzles you, about the topic. Good questions begin with *how*, *why*, *whether* or *should*, because the answers to those take reasoning rather than a lookup.

reveal.text: A topic names an area, a fact is already settled and a question still waits for its answer, so only the sentence that takes a side gives an essay something to prove.

steps.headline: A thesis is a short answer to the question that goes beyond fact, so that evidence can support it and a reasonable reader could still disagree.

lead.text: Now answer the question. A **thesis** is a sentence or two giving your answer, and it differs from everything else in the figure because it takes a side. "Street trees provide shade" is a **fact**: it is true, everyone accepts it, and a whole essay cannot be built on something nobody disputes. The thesis goes a step further and says what should follow from the facts.

That is why people say a thesis must be *arguable*. If a reasonable person could look at the same evidence and conclude something different, then you have something to prove, and a reader has a reason to keep going. If nobody could disagree, you have a topic or a fact in a sentence's clothing.

afterFigure.text: A good habit is to ask, once you've written it, "Who would say no to this, and what would they say?" If you can't think of anyone, the sentence is probably not a thesis yet.

reveal.text: It's true and undisputed, so it can support a thesis but cannot be one.

steps.headline: A thesis can be tested for three qualities: whether it is arguable, whether it is specific, and whether it matters.

lead.text: Compare "Street trees are important" with the longer sentence beside it in the figure. The first can't be disagreed with, so it fails the first test. It is also vague: important to whom, for what, compared with what? And it never says why a reader should care. Those three failures give us three tests, which you can run on any draft thesis.

The stronger sentence passes all three. Someone could reasonably say that cooling centres should come first, so it is arguable. It names the cities, the action and the order, so it is specific. And it bears on how a city spends money and protects people, so it has significance. Notice that being specific doesn't make a thesis longer for its own sake. Each added word is a choice the writer has committed to.

afterFigure.text: Run the tests in that order. A sentence that fails the first has no argument in it, and no amount of detail will rescue it.

steps.headline: Strengthen the thesis "Social media is bad" by running the three tests and repairing each failure.

workedSteps.text: Start with the draft and ask who could disagree. It takes a side, but it hasn't said what "bad" means or for whom.
Plenty of people would dispute it, which means it passes the test that asks whether a reasonable person could disagree. Give the one-word name for that test.
Repair it by choosing a group, an effect and a reason.
workedSteps.math: Heavy evening use of social media harms teenagers' sleep, because notifications keep them alert.

workedSteps.text: Check significance by asking what follows if it is true. It points toward a change in how schools or families handle evening phone use.

steps.headline: Now repair "Libraries are useful" in the same way.

workedSteps.text: The sentence is true, and nobody would dispute it, so it fails the test of being arguable. It is a fact, not a thesis.
Choose one library, one change and one reason, so that someone could say no.
workedSteps.math: Our town library should open on Sunday afternoons, because that is when working families can use it.

workedSteps.text: The sentence is now specific because it names the library, the action and the group. Name the test that asks whether a sentence says exactly what, for whom and when.

steps.headline: A thesis has to fit the length you have, and a first thesis is a working one that the draft is allowed to change.

lead.text: The [[word budget|A plan for how many words each part of a piece gets. Met in 'Reader, purpose and form'.]] returns here, because a thesis can be good and still too big. "Social media has transformed society" is arguable, but nobody can support it in 1,200 words. A useful check is to count the claims you'd need to prove and divide the body's words among them. If each claim gets fewer than about 300 words, the thesis needs narrowing.

It helps to treat your first thesis as a **working thesis**. Writing the draft will teach you things, and you may find that the evidence supports a smaller claim, or a different one. Changing the thesis then isn't a failure, since the thesis is there to make the piece answer something, and you're allowed to improve the answer.

afterFigure.text: The one thing to avoid is drifting: if the draft's argument has changed, rewrite the thesis to match, rather than leaving the old sentence at the top.

reveal.text: The strongest candidate takes a side, names what should change and gives a reason, so it passes all three tests.
At 320 words per claim the thesis is workable, whereas a thesis needing eight claims would leave about 120 words each.

lessons.orientation: Turn a topic into a guiding question, write an arguable thesis and test it.
lessons.nextAction: Order the parts of an essay and a report in the way that suits the reader.

blocks.text: Here is a topic: street trees. You could read about them for a week and fill pages with true facts about shade, root systems and species, and at the end you'd have a heap of material and still no piece, because nothing in the topic tells you which of those facts matter.

What turns the heap into an essay is a decision about what you're trying to find out, followed by a sentence that says what you think the answer is. That sentence has to carry everything after it, so you'll want a way to test it before you draft, both for whether it gives the essay something to prove and for whether it is too big for the words you have.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to turn a topic into a question and write a thesis that is arguable, specific and significant.
intro.whyItMatters: A thesis that nobody could dispute leaves a long piece with nothing to prove, and a draft with no thesis simply piles up facts.

recap.keyIdea: A topic becomes a guiding question, and the question's answer, stated so that a reasonable person could dispute it, is the thesis.

blocks.text: A topic gives you a place to look, a question tells you what to look for, and a thesis is your answer, stated so that evidence can support it. To test a draft thesis, ask whether it is arguable, whether it is specific and whether it says why it matters, and check that it is small enough for the body's word budget. Treat the first version as a working thesis and revise it when the draft teaches you something.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns the thesis into an order for the parts of the piece.

lessons.title: Structure and outline

reveal.text: A reader who may stop early needs the answer at the top, which is the main idea of a report's order.

steps.headline: The order you found things out is rarely the order a reader needs them in.

lead.text: Your notes follow your research: you read about cooling centres first, then found a study, then noticed the cost, and only at the end decided what you thought. That is a perfectly good way to *think*, but a reader who follows it has to wait to learn what the piece is about, and has to guess which of the facts matter.

A reader needs an order built for them, and the tool for building it is an **outline**, a plan of the piece's sections and the one point each makes. In the figure the second list holds exactly the same material as the first, but now each row has a job: the thesis comes first, the reasons build, and an objection is met before the end.

afterFigure.text: Writing the outline costs a few minutes and saves rewriting a draft whose order was wrong. It's much easier to move a line in a list than to move a page of prose.

steps.headline: An essay's sections run from the thesis through the reasons and an objection to a conclusion, and each section makes one point.

lead.text: Here is a standard order for an argumentative essay. The introduction poses the question and states the thesis, so the reader knows from the start what the essay will try to show. The body then gives the reasons in order, one section each, followed by the strongest objection and your reply to it, and the conclusion says what the case adds up to.

Try writing the outline as one sentence per section, as the figure does. That is a strong test of a plan, because a section you can't summarise in a sentence usually doesn't yet have a point. It also lets you check, before drafting, that every row helps answer the question from your thesis.

afterFigure.text: The objection comes after the reasons for a practical reason: the reader has by then seen your case, so the objection and your reply read as testing it. We'll look at how to answer it in the lesson on counterargument.

steps.headline: A report reverses the order and opens with the answer, and this habit is called answer first.

lead.text: A report's reader is making a decision, so the report starts where the essay ends. The **answer first** order opens with a summary that holds the recommendation, then gives the background, the findings, the options and the next steps. The reader who stops after the first paragraph still has the answer, and the reader who continues finds the support in the order they would ask for it.

Look at the figure and notice what moves. The essay's conclusion becomes the report's summary, the essay's reasons become findings, and the essay's objection becomes the options, since a decision-maker wants to know what else could be done. The material is the same, and only the reader's need decides where each part goes.

afterFigure.text: This is not a rule about tidiness. It's a response to how reports are used: they're skimmed, forwarded and read in the gap between two meetings, so the order has to work even when the reader stops early.

reveal.text: Answer first puts the finding where the reader who stops early will still see it.

steps.headline: Within a section, reasons can be ordered by dependence, by time or by importance, and the choice should follow the argument.

lead.text: Once you have the sections, you still have to decide the order of the reasons inside them, and there are three common principles. When one reason needs another, order them by **dependence**, so that each prepares the next: the claim that cooler streets mean less illness only makes sense after you've shown that shade cools the street. When the reasons are events, order them by **time**. And when they're independent, order them by importance, often putting the strongest first or last.

The mistake to avoid is the middle position by default. A strong reason buried between two weak ones is easy to skip over, and a writer who has no reason for the order usually has the wrong one. Ask of each pair, "does the reader need this one before that one?" and let the answer, not the order of your notes, decide.

afterFigure.text: This is the **claim order** of the piece, and it is worth writing into the outline as numbers before you draft.

diagram.alt: Three ways to order reasons: by dependence, where each reason needs the one before; by time, along the order of events; and by importance, ranked from strongest to weakest.

steps.headline: Order three reasons for the street-tree thesis: centres reach few, shade cools, cooler streets mean less illness.

workedSteps.text: The reasons are numbered 1 (cooling centres reach only people who travel to them), 2 (shade lowers street temperatures) and 3 (cooler streets mean less heat illness). Ask which reason needs no other to be understood. Reason 2 is a plain claim about the street, so it can come first.
Reason 3 depends on it, because cooler streets only matter once shade has made them cooler. Which numbered reason has to come first of the three?
Reason 1 compares trees with the alternative, so it needs both of the others and goes last.
Write the outline as one sentence per section: shade cools, cooler streets protect, centres reach fewer people.

steps.headline: Order a five-section report on switching suppliers: findings, summary and recommendation, next steps, background, options.

workedSteps.text: The reader may stop early, so the summary and recommendation come first.
Background tells the reader what situation we are deciding in, so it comes next.
The reader needs to know what was found before choosing between options. Which section comes third?
Options follow the findings, and next steps end the report.

reveal.text: Dependence is the strongest reason to fix an order, because swapping the two would leave the reader lost.
Because findings carry the evidence, they usually take the largest share, while the summary stays short.

lessons.orientation: Order the sections of an essay and of a report, and order reasons within them.
lessons.nextAction: Write a topic sentence that makes a claim, and keep a paragraph on one point.

blocks.text: Your notes on street trees are in the order you found things out: first a piece on cooling centres, then a study of shade and heat illness, then a point about cost, and only at the end the thought that trees should come first. If you followed that order in the piece itself, the reader would spend three pages waiting to learn what you think.

The order you discovered things in is seldom the order a reader needs them in, and what a reader needs depends on what they will do with the piece. A tutor reading an essay and a manager reading a report want the same material arranged quite differently, and once you can see why, you can plan the sections of either one, and the order of the reasons inside each section, before you write any prose.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to order the sections of an essay and a report, and the reasons inside them.
intro.whyItMatters: A good order is the cheapest repair in writing, because it is made in an outline before any prose has to be moved.

recap.keyIdea: An outline orders a piece for its reader: an essay builds from thesis to conclusion, a report puts the answer first, and reasons are ordered by dependence, time or importance.

blocks.text: The order of discovery is rarely the order of reading, so you plan the sections in an outline with one sentence for each. An essay runs from thesis through reasons and an objection to its conclusion, and a report reverses that to put the recommendation first. Within a section, the reasons follow dependence, time or importance, and you choose the one that stops the reader being lost.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson goes inside a section and asks what makes a paragraph do one job.

lessons.title: Paragraphs that do one job

steps.headline: A paragraph makes one claim, and a topic sentence is the sentence that states it.

lead.text: Read the paragraph in the opening figure and ask what it is for. Its first sentence says that shaded streets stay cooler, and everything after it either shows that or explains it. A paragraph is the unit in which you make one claim and support it, which is why its length should be decided by the claim and not by how many lines look right on a page.

The sentence that states the claim is the **topic sentence**, and it usually comes first, because a reader who knows the claim can see what each following sentence is doing. Notice that it is a *claim* and not just a subject: "Shaded streets stay cooler than unshaded ones" says something that could be checked, whereas "This paragraph is about temperature" only names where we are.

afterFigure.text: Most weak paragraphs have a defect you can name here: they open with a fact or a quotation and never say what it is for, so the reader has to guess the claim.

steps.headline: A paragraph has unity when every sentence supports its one claim, and a sentence that supports another claim has to move.

lead.text: Sentence 4 is a good sentence and probably a useful fact. The trouble is that it supports a *different* claim, one about cost, and a reader following the argument about temperature now has to stop and wonder why money has appeared. When every sentence in a paragraph supports its one claim, we say the paragraph has **unity**, and a sentence that breaks it has to go somewhere else.

The fix is usually to move it rather than to delete it. In the figure the cost sentence leaves the temperature paragraph and becomes the start of a new one with its own claim, which is the right outcome whenever the sentence is worth keeping. You may find that it opens a paragraph that your outline lacked, and that is often a sign the outline was missing a reason.

afterFigure.text: Two claims in one paragraph is the same fault seen from the other side. If a paragraph needs two topic sentences, it's two paragraphs.

reveal.text: Unity is judged against the claim, so you can't check it until you have written the claim down.

steps.headline: A good topic sentence states a claim the rest of the paragraph supports, and it does not announce, ask or quote.

lead.text: It helps to compare the common ways of opening a paragraph. "This paragraph discusses temperature" announces and tells the reader nothing they could use. "Do trees cool streets?" asks, and leaves the reader to wait for the answer. A bare quotation or a statistic offers evidence before there is a claim for it to support. The sentence that works says what the paragraph will prove, in a form that can be checked.

A reliable test is to read only the topic sentences of your essay, one after another. Those sentences should make a short version of the whole argument, and if they don't, then either some paragraphs lack a claim or the claims don't follow from one another. We call that a *reverse outline*, and it is the most useful tool you will meet in the lesson on revising the whole.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the test also protects your word budget: a paragraph with no claim tends to wander, and wandering is how a section runs out of room.

steps.headline: Give a topic sentence to a paragraph that holds only evidence and an explanation.

workedSteps.text: The paragraph begins: "A shaded street measured 31 °C and an unshaded one 36 °C. The canopy blocks sunlight before it reaches the pavement." Both sentences are about why shaded streets are cooler.
The paragraph has evidence and an explanation but no sentence that says what they prove. Give the one name for the sentence that states a paragraph's claim.
Write it as a claim that the evidence supports.
workedSteps.math: Shaded streets stay cooler than unshaded ones.

workedSteps.text: Put it first, so the reader knows what the evidence is for.

steps.headline: A paragraph is coherent when its sentences follow in an order a reader can see, usually from the general claim to the specific evidence and then onward.

lead.text: Unity is about what's in the paragraph, and **coherence** is about how the sentences are arranged. The usual arrangement runs from general to specific: the claim, then the evidence, then an explanation of why the evidence supports the claim. That order lets the reader meet each sentence knowing why it is there, which is the given-before-new habit applied to a whole paragraph.

The last sentence is often a link to the next paragraph's claim. In the figure the link is the thought that cooler streets should mean less heat illness, which is exactly what the next paragraph will argue. A link of that kind does the reader a service, because it tells them where the argument is going before they get there, and it doesn't need a stock phrase to work.

afterFigure.text: Connecting words such as "so", "because" and "however" help, but only when the ideas really do connect that way. The order does most of the work.

lessons.orientation: Write a topic sentence that makes a claim, and move a sentence that breaks a paragraph's unity.
lessons.nextAction: Choose evidence for a claim, introduce it, explain it, and report a percentage correctly.

blocks.text: Here are five sentences about street trees. The first says that shaded streets stay cooler, the second gives two temperature readings, the third explains the gap between them, the fourth says that planting a tree costs a few hundred pounds, and the fifth says that trees help at the hottest time of day. Each of them is true, and yet read together as a paragraph they feel slightly off.

You can probably point to the sentence that spoils it, and what you're using when you do is a sense of what the paragraph is for. Once that sense has names and a test, you can write a first sentence that tells the reader what a paragraph claims, and see at once which of the sentences after it support the claim and which belong somewhere else.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a topic sentence that makes a claim, and cut or move a sentence that breaks a paragraph's unity.
intro.whyItMatters: Most readers decide whether a long piece is clear paragraph by paragraph, so a paragraph that does one job is where clarity starts.

recap.keyIdea: A paragraph makes one claim, stated in a topic sentence, and every sentence in it supports that claim in an order the reader can follow.

blocks.text: A paragraph is the unit in which you make one claim and support it, so it opens with a topic sentence that states the claim rather than announcing a subject. Unity asks that every sentence supports that claim, and a sentence that supports another claim moves to a paragraph of its own. Coherence arranges what remains from general to specific, and a closing link points to the next claim.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the evidence inside a paragraph and what you say about it.

lessons.title: Evidence and what you say about it

reveal.text: The number is evidence, and evidence needs a sentence of the writer's own to connect it to the claim.

steps.headline: Evidence does not speak for itself: the reader needs a lead-in, the evidence and a sentence that ties it back to the claim.

lead.text: Look at the first view of the opening figure. The claim is there and so is a number, but a reader who sees "23.5%" has to decide for themselves whether that's large or small, and what it has to do with cycling routes. **Evidence** is anything that supports a claim, whether data, a quotation, an example or an authority, and the writer's mistake is to assume it is self-explanatory.

The second view adds the two missing moves. A **signal phrase**, such as "According to our survey", tells the reader where the evidence comes from before they meet it. After the evidence, a sentence of **analysis** says what it shows and why that supports the claim. Here the analysis is that nearly one commuter in four is a group large enough to call many, and it is the writer's sentence, not the survey's.

afterFigure.text: Analysis is where an argument happens. Without it, a paragraph is a claim next to a pile of facts, and the reader does the thinking you were supposed to do.

reveal.text: The signal phrase also marks the point where someone else's material begins, which keeps it separate from your own claim.

steps.headline: Each piece of evidence takes the same three moves in order: lead in, show it, and tie it back.

lead.text: The order matters because of what the reader needs at each point. Before the evidence they need to know what kind of thing it is and who says it, which is the lead-in. Then they need the evidence in a form they can check. After it they need the *connection*, which is the sentence beginning something like "That is nearly one in four", and it should refer to the claim so the paragraph returns to its point.

A piece of evidence introduced and explained this way usually takes two or three sentences, which is why a paragraph tends to hold only one or two pieces. Packing in five items with no comment feels thorough but proves less than a single item that is properly explained.

afterFigure.text: A good check is to cover the claim and read the analysis alone. If it doesn't say, in some form, what the claim was, the tie back is too loose.

steps.headline: Quote when the exact words are the evidence, paraphrase when only the idea matters, and give a number when size matters.

lead.text: Evidence comes in different forms, and the form should follow the job. Use a **quotation** when the exact wording is the point, for example when you're analysing how someone phrased something, and keep it short. Use a **paraphrase**, a restatement in your own words with the source named, when only the idea matters, which is most of the time. Use a **number** when the question is *how much* or *how many*.

A common weakness is quoting by default. A long quotation can be the writer avoiding the work of saying what the source means, and the reader tends to skim it. If you can say the idea clearly in a sentence of your own, do so and name the source, and keep quotation marks for the phrases that earn them.

afterFigure.text: The same rule holds for numbers: give the figure and what it is a figure of, and don't leave it floating.

steps.headline: Report 47 of 200 respondents as a percentage.

workedSteps.text: A percentage is a share out of 100, so start by writing the share as a fraction of the whole group.
Divide to get the decimal. Give the decimal that you get.
Multiply by 100 to turn the decimal into a percentage.
Report it with its base, so the reader knows what the percentage is of.

steps.headline: Report 36 of 150 respondents as a percentage.

workedSteps.text: Write the share as a fraction of the whole group.
Divide to get the decimal.
Multiply by 100 to give the percentage. Work out the percentage.

steps.headline: A careful writer also says what the evidence cannot show, which keeps the claim in proportion to it.

lead.text: The grid in the figure makes the survey result easy to see: 47 filled squares out of 200. It also shows its limits. The squares record what respondents *said*, which is not the same as what they would do, and 200 commuters may not represent a whole city. Nothing in the figure says why they answered as they did.

Saying so in a sentence is not a weakness. It tells the reader you know the weight the evidence can bear, and so it makes the rest of your claims easier to believe. Report the base along with the percentage, so a reader can judge, because "23.5%" means little until they know it is 47 out of 200 and not 4 out of 17.

afterFigure.text: In the next lesson this habit becomes a technique: the qualifier, a word that sets a claim at the strength the evidence allows.

blocks.text: A paragraph claims that many commuters would cycle if the route were safer, and the next sentence reads: "23.5% of respondents said they would cycle with a protected lane." The number is accurate, and it sits where it should, straight after the claim it is meant to support.

Yet the paragraph ends there, and it is worth asking whether a reader who reaches the number has been given everything they need. Working out what a writer owes the reader at that point lets you take any figure, quotation or example and make it support a claim in a way the reader can see, and report a percentage in a form they can check.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to introduce a piece of evidence, explain how it supports a claim, and report a percentage correctly.
intro.whyItMatters: A paragraph of well-chosen evidence still persuades no one if the reader is left to work out what it means.

recap.keyIdea: Evidence is introduced with a signal phrase, shown, and then explained in a sentence of analysis that ties it back to the claim.

blocks.text: Evidence does not speak for itself, so each piece takes a lead-in that names its source, the evidence itself, and a sentence of analysis that says why it supports the claim. You choose the form by the job: a quotation when the wording matters, a paraphrase when the idea does, a number when the size does. A percentage is the count divided by the base and multiplied by 100, and it is reported with the base so that the reader can judge its weight.

lessons.title: Answering the other side

reveal.text: A reasoned objection is one of the things a good argument has to meet, rather than avoid.

steps.headline: State the objection in the strongest form a thoughtful critic would give it, because that is the only version your reader will believe you have answered.

lead.text: A **counterargument** is a reason a reasonable reader might give against your thesis, and a persuasive piece meets it instead of hoping it won't be raised. The reader who thinks of the objection while reading and finds no reply will conclude that you hadn't thought of it, or hoped they wouldn't.

The temptation is to answer an easy version. "Street trees are ugly" is simple to reply to, but nobody weighing the policy would stop there, and a reply to it persuades no one. The version in the figure's second view, that trees need water and water is scarce, is the one a careful critic would actually raise. State that one fairly, in a form its holder would accept as their own, and your reply will carry weight.

afterFigure.text: A practical test is to ask someone who disagrees with your thesis what their best reason is, and to write down what they say rather than what you expected.

steps.headline: Grant what is right in the objection, then show why the thesis still stands.

lead.text: Once the objection is stated, the temptation is to deny all of it. A better move starts with a **concession**, granting what is true in the objection: yes, trees need water, and in a hot climate that is a real cost. This doesn't weaken the argument. It shows the reader you are weighing the evidence and not defending a position at any price, which makes your later claims more credible.

Then comes the reply, which says why the thesis still holds. Some species need little water once established, and shade reduces other cooling demands, so the cost is smaller than the objection suggests. A common pattern is therefore three sentences: the objection, "that is true, but", and the reason the thesis survives.

afterFigure.text: Where the paragraph goes matters less than that it comes where the reader will raise the objection, usually after your reasons and before the conclusion.

steps.headline: A qualifier limits a claim to the cases and strength the evidence supports.

lead.text: The objection also tells you something about your own claim. If trees need water, then "cities in hot climates" is too broad, since some hot cities are short of water. You can respond by qualifying the claim, which means adding a word or phrase that sets its limits: "in hot but water-rich cities", or "usually". Such a word or phrase is a **qualifier**, and Stephen Toulmin gave it a place in his scheme of an argument, next to the claim and its grounds, in *The Uses of Argument* (1958).

The skill is to fit the strength of the claim to the strength of the evidence. "Trees always fix heat" outruns any evidence you could have. "Trees might sometimes do something" is safe because it says nothing. The middle version, which says where and how often, is one a reader can weigh and a critic can still challenge, and that is what a thesis is for.

afterFigure.text: Qualifying is not hedging for its own sake. Each qualifier should correspond to something the evidence or the objection actually showed.

steps.headline: Qualify the claim "Trees fix heat in every city" so that the evidence could support it.

workedSteps.text: Ask where the claim is least likely to hold. Water-poor cities are the obvious case, so add a limit on where.
Ask how often. A single street may stay hot, so soften "fix" to a claim about the usual result.
Name the kind of word or phrase that limits a claim in this way.
Read the result back to check that a claim is still being made.
workedSteps.math: In hot but water-rich cities, street trees usually lower temperatures.

steps.headline: Now qualify "Cities in hot climates should plant street trees before cooling centres" in the same way.

workedSteps.text: The objection was about water, so the first limit is on where.
A second limit is on how firm the advice is: street trees should come first only where the evidence supports it.
The finished claim has two limits. Pick out the words that set them.

steps.headline: Put the objection where the reader will raise it, and stop qualifying when the claim begins to disappear.

lead.text: There are two last decisions. The first is placement. In an essay the objection and reply usually come after the reasons, as the outline in an earlier lesson showed, because the reader has by then seen your case and is ready to test it. If a sensible reader would raise the objection earlier, say right after you state the thesis, deal with it there.

The second is restraint. Every qualifier narrows the claim, and a claim hedged with "might", "perhaps" and "to some extent" says nothing that could be wrong, so nothing that is worth reading. Add a qualifier when the evidence or the objection calls for it, and stop when the claim can still be disagreed with.

reveal.text: The best-qualified claim limits where and how often, and still says something a critic could dispute.
The word usually limits how often the claim holds, which is what a qualifier does.

lessons.nextAction: Choose the connective that fits two sentences, and write an opening and an ending that do work.

blocks.text: Here is a thesis: cities in hot climates should plant street trees before building cooling centres. A thoughtful critic would reply that trees need water, and that in hot climates water is often scarce, and on the water the critic is simply right.

What should an argument do with an objection like that, when the critic is partly right? The answer decides whether a thesis survives a careful reader, and it also tells you how far your own claim should reach, since the places where an objection bites are the places where the claim needs a limit.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to state the strongest objection to your thesis fairly, answer it, and qualify the claim to the strength the evidence allows.
intro.whyItMatters: Readers raise the objection whether or not you do, so an argument that meets it first is the one they believe.

recap.keyIdea: A strong piece states the best objection fairly, grants what is right in it, replies, and qualifies its claim to the strength the evidence allows.

blocks.text: The objection to answer is the one a thoughtful critic would make, stated fairly enough that its holder would accept it. You concede what is true in it and give the reason the thesis still stands, and where the objection exposes a limit in the claim you add a qualifier to fit. Stop qualifying when the claim can no longer be disputed, because a claim nobody can dispute has nothing left to prove.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to how a piece begins and ends, and how its sentences connect.

lessons.title: Openings, endings and transitions

steps.headline: A transition is a word or phrase that tells the reader how a sentence relates to the one before it.

lead.text: Take the sentence "Shade lowers street temperatures." and look at what could follow it. If the next sentence says that trees need water, it cuts against the first, and the word that tells the reader so is *however*. If it says that cooling demand falls, it follows from the first, and the word is *therefore*. A **transition** is a word or phrase of this kind, and its job is to name the **relation** between two sentences so the reader doesn't have to guess it.

The relation can be contrast, cause, example or addition, and the figure gives one connective for each: *however*, *therefore*, *for instance* and *moreover*. They are not interchangeable. Each says something definite, which is why choosing one is a matter of deciding what the relation actually is, and only then choosing the word.

afterFigure.text: That order matters. Writers who reach for a connective before deciding the relation often pick one that sounds like argument but says the wrong thing.

reveal.text: The connective for contrast announces that the next sentence pulls the other way.

steps.headline: A connective makes a claim about the relation, so it is wrong when the relation isn't there.

lead.text: A common misuse is *however* for any change of subject. "Shade lowers temperatures. However, the survey had 200 respondents." There is no contrast here, only a new topic, and the reader looks for a conflict that never arrives. *Therefore* has the opposite problem: it claims that the second sentence follows from the first, so using it where the second sentence merely comes next asserts a link you haven't shown.

Often the better choice is no connective at all, with the relation carried by the sentences themselves. When two sentences really do follow one another in a clear line, a transition can be unnecessary, and a thicket of *moreover* and *furthermore* only slows the reader down. Use one when the relation would otherwise be hard to see, and be sure it is the right one.

afterFigure.text: A quick check: remove the connective and ask whether the reader would still see the relation. If they would, you may not need it.

reveal.text: An added advantage points the same way as the first, so the connective for addition fits and the one for contrast does not.

steps.headline: Choose a connective for "The street is shaded. ___ it stays cool."

workedSteps.text: Ask what the second sentence does with the first. A shaded street stays cool because of the shade, so the second follows from the first.
Match the relation to a connective: contrast is however, example is for instance, addition is moreover, and cause is the one that remains. Pick the connective for cause.
Read the pair aloud to check that the claim of cause is one you can defend.
workedSteps.math: The street is shaded. Therefore it stays cool.

steps.headline: Now choose one for "Shade lowers temperatures. ___, one shaded street measured five degrees cooler."

workedSteps.text: The second sentence gives a case of the first, so the relation is an example.
The connective for an example is for instance, or for example. Give the connective.

steps.headline: An opening brings the reader from their world to your question, by way of a context, a problem and the thesis.

lead.text: The opening has one job, which is to get the reader from wherever they were to your thesis. A reliable path goes in three steps. A **context** says where the reader already is: summers are getting hotter. A **problem** names what is unresolved: cooling centres reach only the people who travel to them. And the thesis answers it. Each step narrows what the reader is thinking about until they are ready for the claim.

Avoid the broad opening. "Since the dawn of time, humans have sought relief from heat" is true of everything and does no work, and it spends words from a limited budget before the reader has met your question. Start from the context your reader actually has, and reach the thesis within the first few sentences.

afterFigure.text: An opening of about a tenth of the piece is typical, as the word budget in the first lesson suggested.

steps.headline: An ending says what follows from the argument and what remains open, and it does not repeat the introduction.

lead.text: When you reach the end, the reader already knows what you argued, so repeating the introduction wastes their attention. What they don't yet have is the answer to "so what?". An **ending** therefore says what follows from the argument: if the thesis holds, what should a city do? Then it may say what remains open, the part the evidence did not settle, which is honest and often interesting.

Two mistakes are worth avoiding. One is introducing a new argument at the very end, which the reader has no room left to weigh. The other is the apology, "of course, this is only one view", which weakens a claim you've just spent pages supporting. The qualifiers belong inside the argument, where the evidence called for them.

afterFigure.text: A good ending can be a short paragraph. It does not need to sound like an ending, only to leave the reader knowing what to do or think next.

reveal.text: The ending's job is to look onward from the argument, not to restate it.
An opening of this size has room for a context, a problem and a thesis, with nothing left over for a long run-up.

lessons.orientation: Choose the connective that fits the relation between two sentences, and write an opening and an ending that do work.
lessons.nextAction: Use a reverse outline to find problems in structure and order the stages of revision.

blocks.text: Put these two sentences side by side: "Shade lowers street temperatures." "Trees need water." Each is true, and the reader has to work out alone how the second bears on the first, which is easy here but much harder six pages into an argument.

The small word you put between them settles that question for the reader, and it can just as easily settle it wrongly, making the second sentence look like a consequence of the first when it is really a difficulty. Choosing that word with care, and knowing what the first and last paragraphs of a piece have to do, is how you keep a reader with your argument from its opening sentence to its end.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose a connective that fits the relation between two sentences, and write an opening and an ending that do work.
intro.whyItMatters: Readers follow an argument through its joins, and a wrong connective sends them the wrong way.

recap.keyIdea: A connective names the relation between sentences, so choose the relation first; an opening leads to the thesis and an ending says what follows from it.

blocks.text: Transitions such as however, therefore, for instance and moreover each name a relation, and they are right only when the relation is there. An opening moves from a context the reader holds, through a problem, to the thesis, while an ending says what follows from the argument and what the evidence left open, without repeating the introduction.

lessons.title: Revising the whole

reveal.text: A list written from the draft shows what the draft actually says, which can differ from what you planned.

steps.headline: A reverse outline is a list of what each paragraph of a draft actually says, made after the draft.

lead.text: An ordinary outline is made before writing and says what you mean to do. A **reverse outline** works the other way round: you read the finished draft and write one line for each paragraph, saying what it actually says. The two can differ, and the gap between them is where most structural faults hide, because a writer rereading their own prose tends to read what they meant.

The figure shows the list for a seven-paragraph draft on street trees. Read down it as you would read a plan and ask three things. Does it follow the plan you meant to follow? Does any line repeat an earlier one? Does the argument jump from one point to another without a link? Here paragraphs 3 and 5 both say that shade lowers temperatures, which no one would notice from inside the paragraphs but which is plain in the list.

afterFigure.text: Making the list is cheap, a few minutes, and it turns a long piece into something you can see at once, as a map shows a country.

steps.headline: Revise from the whole down: argument and structure first, then paragraphs, then sentences, and proofreading last.

lead.text: Once the list shows problems, you can move, merge, cut or add paragraphs. Those are changes to the whole piece, and we call revision at that scale **global revision**, in contrast to **local revision**, which changes sentences and words. The order matters because each larger change can make smaller work pointless. If you polish the sentences of paragraph 5 and then merge it into paragraph 3, the polishing is gone.

So the stages run from largest to smallest: argument, structure, paragraphs, sentences and proofreading. The common mistake is to start at the bottom, correcting commas in a draft whose argument is still moving, because it feels productive and the errors are easy to see. Large problems are harder to see and harder to fix, which is exactly why they should come first.

afterFigure.text: Treat each stage as a pass with a single question. You'll often find that a stage needs no change, and then it takes minutes.

steps.headline: Put these revision jobs in order: fix a comma, reorder two sections, check the thesis against the evidence, tighten a sentence, merge two paragraphs.

workedSteps.text: Start with the largest question: does the thesis match the evidence? That is the argument.
Next comes the order of sections. Revision that changes the argument or the sections is global. Give the one word that names this scale.
Then paragraphs, such as merging two, then sentences, such as tightening one, and the comma last.

steps.headline: Merge paragraphs 3 and 5, which run 180 and 150 words, into one paragraph of 200 words, and find how many words you save.

workedSteps.text: Add the two paragraphs to see what they hold now.
The merged paragraph says the same thing in 200 words.
Subtract to find the words saved.

steps.headline: Revise until a pass stops improving the piece, and treat the outline as a tool rather than a finished plan.

lead.text: Revision does not run for ever. At each stage you ask whether the changes you are making still improve the piece, and when they no longer do you move on or stop. A writer who has made the structure sound and the paragraphs clear, and who is now swapping synonyms, has stopped improving and started fiddling.

It also helps to remember that the reverse outline is a tool, not a plan to finish before you write. The ordinary outline you made earlier is allowed to change as the draft teaches you things, and the reverse outline records where it has actually changed. Both are working documents, and the second one is the check on the first.

afterFigure.text: Reading a draft aloud is a good tool at the sentence stage, because awkward sentences are easier to hear than to see.

reveal.text: The argument is the largest unit, so changes to it can make every later stage's work pointless.
The list is a map for deciding where to merge, cut or move material, and a repeated point is a clear case for merging.

blocks.text: A draft on street trees has seven paragraphs, and when you read it through it seems fine, since every paragraph is decent and every sentence reads well. That impression is worth less than it feels, because a writer rereading their own prose tends to see what they meant to write rather than what is on the page.

Revising a long piece starts with a way of seeing the draft as a reader will, as a whole rather than one sentence at a time, and then deciding which problems to fix first. Get that order wrong and you can spend an afternoon polishing paragraphs that the next change will cut.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to make a reverse outline of a draft and order the stages of revision from largest to smallest.
intro.whyItMatters: Most of what weakens a long piece is a structural fault, and structural faults are invisible while you're polishing sentences.

recap.keyIdea: A reverse outline shows what a draft says, and revision then runs from the argument and structure down to paragraphs, sentences and proofreading.

blocks.text: A reverse outline lists what each paragraph of the draft actually says, so you can see where it repeats, jumps or departs from the plan. You then revise globally before locally, because a change to the argument or structure can undo any work done on sentences. You stop at the stage where changes no longer improve the piece.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson goes down to the sentence, where the aim is to say the same thing in fewer words.

lessons.title: Clear and short sentences

reveal.text: Most of the slack in a draft sits in phrases that use several words where one would do, which is why a large cut can leave every fact in place.

steps.headline: Every word should earn its place, which means cutting what the meaning does not need and keeping everything it does.

lead.text: Look at the sentence in the figure: "At this point in time, the committee made a decision to approve the plan." Fourteen words, and the reader gains nothing from the first five. "At this point in time" does the work of *now* and here not even that, since the sentence doesn't need a time at all. George Orwell put the rule in plain terms in "Politics and the English Language" (1946): "If it is possible to cut a word out, always cut it out."

Orwell's rule is a good habit, and it has a limit, which is meaning. The test of a cut is whether every fact, number and name is still there afterwards. The marked view of the figure shows the three possible verdicts for each part of a sentence: cut what adds nothing, keep what carries the meaning, and replace what says it in too many words.

afterFigure.text: So a cut is not a deletion made at random. It's a decision, part by part, about whether the reader loses anything.

steps.headline: Turning a verb into a noun, as in 'make a decision', is a common source of extra words, and the single verb says the same thing.

lead.text: The phrase "made a decision" has three words where one will do. The action, deciding, has been turned into a noun, *decision*, and a weak verb, *made*, has been added to carry it. This process is called **nominalisation**, and it is one of the commonest ways a sentence grows longer without growing clearer.

The cure is to look for the action hiding in the noun and put it back as a verb: "made a decision" becomes *decided*, "gave consideration to" becomes *considered*, and "conducted an investigation of" becomes *investigated*. Notice that nothing is lost. The sentence is shorter, the verb does more work, and the reader reaches the action sooner.

afterFigure.text: Plain-language guides for government writing give the same advice, because readers in a hurry find the verb faster than the noun.

steps.headline: A clear sentence puts the actor in the subject and the action in the verb.

lead.text: The second habit concerns who is doing what. In a clear sentence the **actor**, the person or thing that does something, is the subject, and the **action** is the verb, so the reader meets who did what in the order they'd expect. "The committee decided to approve the plan" does this. "A decision was made to approve the plan" doesn't, and it leaves the reader to ask who decided.

The passive voice isn't always wrong, since sometimes the actor is unknown or unimportant. The trouble is when it hides an actor the reader needs, or when a nominalisation and a passive combine, as in "consideration was given to the plan". Recast it by asking who did the thing, make that person the subject, and use a single verb.

afterFigure.text: Do check, after recasting, that you haven't dropped a fact. If the original named a date or a number, the new sentence must too.

steps.headline: A 150-word paragraph is cut to 100 words. What percentage of it was cut?

workedSteps.text: Start by finding how many words were removed. Give that number.
Divide the words removed by the original length, because the percentage is a share of what you started with.
Multiply by 100 and round to one decimal place.

steps.headline: Cut a 360-word section by one quarter and find how many words remain.

workedSteps.text: A quarter of 360 is the share to remove.
Subtract the words cut from the original length.

steps.headline: A cut is only good if no fact is lost, and shorter is not always better.

lead.text: Before you cut, list the facts the passage carries: the numbers, the names and the claims. After cutting, check the list. A paragraph cut by a third that has lost its only number has not been tightened, it's been damaged, and the check takes under a minute. Cutting for the sake of a target without that check is the most common way revision makes a piece worse.

Shorter isn't automatically better either. Strip away every connective and every qualifier and the prose becomes a string of assertions that the reader can't follow, and a qualifier you removed may have been the thing keeping a claim honest. The aim is economy, which is using only the words the meaning needs, and not as few words as possible.

afterFigure.text: A useful target is a stated fraction, such as one third, because it forces you to find the slack. The check afterwards keeps you honest.

reveal.text: The best recast keeps the actor and the object and replaces the noun-plus-verb with a single verb.
Cutting a report by a fraction follows the same two steps as cutting a paragraph: work out what goes, then what is left.

lessons.orientation: Cut a passage by a stated fraction without losing meaning, and recast a nominalised sentence.

blocks.text: Here is a sentence from a draft: "At this point in time, the committee made a decision to approve the plan." It has fourteen words, and every fact in it would survive in a sentence half that length.

Finding the words a sentence can lose is a skill with rules, and so is knowing when to stop, because a cut that removes a fact or a qualifier makes a piece worse however much shorter it gets. With both, you can take a draft that runs over its word budget and bring it in without losing anything the reader needs.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to cut a passage by a stated fraction without losing its facts, and recast a nominalised sentence.
intro.whyItMatters: Short, clear sentences are what a reader notices last, because they make everything else easy to follow.

recap.keyIdea: Cut words the meaning does not need, turn nouns that hide actions back into verbs, and keep the actor in the subject.

blocks.text: A cut is a decision, part by part, about whether the reader loses anything, so you list the facts first and check them afterwards. The commonest slack is a nominalisation, an action turned into a noun and propped up with a weak verb, and the fix is to put the verb back and the actor in the subject. You can set the target as a fraction, and compute it before you start.

lessons.title: A process that finishes

reveal.text: A forward plan gives the last stages whatever days are left, so when research runs long it is revision and proofreading that lose out.

steps.headline: A backward plan starts from the deadline and works back, giving each stage the days it needs, with revision included from the start.

lead.text: Most people plan forwards: start researching, see how it goes, and write when the research feels finished. The trouble is that research never feels finished, so the days run down and revision and proofreading are squeezed into the last one or two. A **backward plan** reverses this. You fix the deadline, subtract the stages that must come last, and let the earlier stages take whatever remains.

The first view of the figure shows a plan for a 3,000-word piece with 14 days: research 3, outline 1, draft 4, revise 4, proofread 2, which adds up to 14. The second view shows the common alternative, in which research takes 8 days and revision gets one. Both spend 14 days; only the first leaves time for the stages that make a draft into a finished piece.

afterFigure.text: The numbers are a sketch and will change. What matters is that revising and proofreading have days of their own before you start.

steps.headline: Feedback is most useful when it answers a question you asked, so ask about something specific.

lead.text: A draft read by someone else tells you what you can't see yourself, but only if you direct the reading. The question "Is it good?" invites a polite yes, and a polite yes gives you nothing to change. **Feedback** is a reader's response to your piece, and it is most useful when it answers a question you asked, such as "What do you think my thesis is?" or "Where did you stop following?".

Look at the two questions in the figure. The first can be answered in a word. The second can only be answered by pointing at a place, and the place is exactly what you need for revising. Ask your reader to say the thesis back in their own words: if it differs from yours, the draft isn't saying what you think it says, and that is the most important thing you can learn.

afterFigure.text: Ask while there's still time to act on the answer. Feedback on the last day can only be admired.

steps.headline: Proofreading is a last pass for errors, done once, after all other revision, and it is easiest aloud.

lead.text: **Proofreading** looks for slips: typing errors, wrong words, missing punctuation, a number that disagrees with a table. It belongs at the very end for a plain reason. Any larger revision rewrites sentences, and every rewritten sentence can bring a new slip, so proofreading before revising is work thrown away.

A reliable method is to read the piece aloud, slowly, once. Your eyes tend to skip over a doubled word because you know what the sentence is meant to say, but your voice stumbles on it. Reading aloud also catches the sentence that is too long for one breath, which you may then fix. If you do find large problems at this stage, treat that as a sign that an earlier stage was cut short, and go back.

afterFigure.text: The plan gives proofreading its own two days, because rested eyes see more than tired ones.

reveal.text: It comes last because earlier changes would introduce new slips.
The days left for the stages that make the piece decide how much you can write and how much you can improve it.

lessons.orientation: Plan a writing schedule backwards from a deadline, and use feedback and proofreading effectively.
lessons.nextAction: Organise a report with the answer first, headings that signpost, and a summary that stands alone.

blocks.text: You have 3,000 words to write and 14 days to write them in. Most people start with the research, since you can't write what you don't know, and plan to begin writing once the research feels finished, which seems sensible because it follows the order the work has to happen in.

The difficulty is that research rarely feels finished, and a plan that only runs forwards has no way of noticing that it is running out of days. Working the schedule out from the deadline instead, and deciding what to ask a reader and when to proofread, is what lets a piece reach its deadline finished instead of merely stopped.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to plan a writing schedule backwards from a deadline, and ask for feedback and proofread so that they help.
intro.whyItMatters: A piece that is planned to finish gets revised, and revision is where most of the improvement comes from.

recap.keyIdea: Work the schedule back from the deadline, ask readers specific questions while you can still act on them, and proofread once, aloud, at the very end.

blocks.text: A backward plan gives revising and proofreading their own days before research expands to fill the time, and it turns a total length into a daily word count you can check. Feedback helps most when you ask a question that points at a place in the draft, and proofreading comes last, because every larger change brings new slips.

lessons.title: The shape of a report

reveal.text: A reader who wants to judge a study needs its question and method before its results, so a research report follows the order in which the work was done.

steps.headline: A decision report puts the answer first, while a research report follows the order in which the study was done.

lead.text: Two readers need two shapes. A decision report serves someone who has to act, so as the earlier lesson on structure showed it opens with the summary and recommendation, then gives the background, findings, options and next steps. Copying the order of a research report into a decision report is a real fault: it makes the manager wait through the method before reaching the recommendation.

A research report serves a reader who wants to judge or repeat the study, and its usual order is **IMRaD**: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. The introduction says what the question is, the methods say how it was answered, the results say what was found and the discussion says what that means. The order follows the work, because that is what this reader will check.

afterFigure.text: When you're given a brief, ask which reader it serves. The answer tells you which shape to use, and the shape tells you where the answer goes.

steps.headline: An executive summary gives the question, the finding, the recommendation and the cost, so that a reader can act without reading further.

lead.text: The opening section of a decision report is its **executive summary**, and it carries more weight than any other part, because many readers will read nothing else. It should say four things: the question the report asked, what was found, what the reader should do, and what doing it costs or saves. Four short sentences can do this, as the example in the figure does.

The test of a summary is that it *stands alone*. Someone who reads only the summary should be able to act and should not need to turn the page to learn what the report was about. This means it cannot refer to "the table below" or use terms the body defines later. It is also written last, since you can't summarise findings you haven't yet written, though it is placed first.

afterFigure.text: As a rough guide, a summary of about a tenth of the report is a good starting budget, as in the first lesson, and many are shorter.

steps.headline: A signpost heading says what the section tells the reader, so that someone skimming the headings gets the argument.

lead.text: Headings are what a busy reader looks at first. A **topic heading** names the subject: "Costs". It tells the reader where something is, but not what it says, so they have to read the section to find out. A **signpost heading** says what the section tells the reader: "Supplier B costs 12% less". The number in this example is invented, and the point is the form.

Read the second set in the figure by itself and you can follow the case without opening a single section: the supplier has been used for six years, B costs less, deliveries are as reliable, and the advice is to switch. A reader who skims gets the finding, and a reader who wants the support knows which section to open. That is what signposting is for.

afterFigure.text: Don't overdo it: a heading that is a full sentence of fifteen words defeats its purpose. Keep it short enough to scan.

steps.headline: Check a summary by giving it to someone who has not read the report and seeing whether they could act.

lead.text: The only reliable test of a summary is to hand it, alone, to a reader who hasn't seen the report. Ask them what the report found and what they would do. If they can answer, the summary works. If they ask what "the options" are or what a figure refers to, it still depends on the body.

The same standard applies to the whole of the answer-first idea. A decision report buries its recommendation when it puts it at the end, and a research report built as a chronicle, "first we read, then we tried", makes the reader reconstruct the finding for themselves. In both cases the remedy is to say what was found where the reader will first look.

afterFigure.text: Revise the summary last, after the body is final, so that its numbers match the body's. The next lesson takes that problem on directly.

reveal.text: A signpost heading gives the reader the point of the section without their opening it.
